title: Human Body Systems
description: How the digestive, circulatory, respiratory, nervous, excretory, and musculoskeletal systems work independently and together to maintain life.

notes.heading: The Digestive System
notes.body: The digestive system breaks down large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood. The journey: Mouth — mechanical digestion by chewing; salivary amylase enzyme begins breaking down starch into maltose. Oesophagus — muscular tube using peristalsis (wave-like contractions) to push food down. Stomach — churns food with hydrochloric acid (kills bacteria, provides optimum pH for protease enzymes) and pepsin (protease that begins protein digestion). Small intestine — the main site of digestion and absorption. Pancreatic enzymes (amylase, protease, lipase) and bile from the liver (emulsifies fats) complete digestion. The inner wall is covered with millions of villi — finger-like projections that massively increase surface area for absorption. Each villus has a network of blood capillaries (absorb glucose, amino acids, water-soluble vitamins) and a lacteal (absorbs fatty acids and glycerol). Large intestine — absorbs remaining water and minerals, forming faeces. Rectum — stores faeces before egestion. Key enzymes: amylase (starch → maltose), protease (protein → amino acids), lipase (fats → fatty acids + glycerol).

notes.heading: The Circulatory System
notes.body: The circulatory system transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste products around the body. The heart is a muscular double pump: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation); the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body (systemic circulation). Each side has an atrium (receives blood) and a ventricle (pumps blood out). The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall because it must pump blood much further (around the entire body). Blood vessels: Arteries — carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; thick muscular walls; narrow lumen. Veins — carry blood back to the heart at low pressure; thin walls with valves to prevent backflow; wider lumen. Capillaries — microscopic vessels (one cell thick) connecting arteries to veins; site of gas and nutrient exchange at tissues. Blood components: Red blood cells (transport oxygen via haemoglobin; no nucleus; biconcave shape), White blood cells (defend against pathogens; part of immune system), Platelets (cell fragments that trigger blood clotting), Plasma (liquid transporting dissolved substances — glucose, amino acids, CO₂, urea, hormones).

notes.heading: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange
notes.body: The respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. Air pathway: Nose/mouth → trachea (windpipe, supported by C-shaped cartilage rings to prevent collapse) → bronchi (two branches, one to each lung) → bronchioles (many smaller branches) → alveoli. Alveoli are the site of gas exchange. They are tiny air sacs — millions per lung — with four key adaptations: (1) Large surface area (total surface ~70 m²). (2) Very thin walls — one cell thick epithelium, minimising diffusion distance. (3) Rich blood supply — surrounded by dense capillary networks maintaining a steep concentration gradient. (4) Moist inner surface — gases dissolve before diffusing. Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli (high concentration) into the blood (low concentration). Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli to be exhaled. Breathing (ventilation): The diaphragm contracts and flattens, and intercostal muscles lift the rib cage up and out. This increases chest volume, lowering pressure, so air rushes in (inhalation). Exhalation is largely passive — muscles relax, chest volume decreases, pressure rises, air is pushed out.

notes.heading: The Nervous System
notes.body: The nervous system enables rapid communication between different parts of the body using electrical impulses. It has two main divisions: (1) Central Nervous System (CNS) — the brain and spinal cord. The brain processes information and coordinates responses; the spinal cord relays impulses to and from the brain. (2) Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) — all nerves connecting the CNS to the rest of the body. A nerve cell (neuron) is specialised to transmit electrical signals: dendrites receive signals; the cell body contains the nucleus; the axon carries impulses away over long distances (up to 1 metre); the myelin sheath insulates the axon, speeding up transmission; axon terminals pass the signal to the next neuron. At synapses (gaps between neurons), the signal is transmitted chemically — neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across the gap. Reflex actions are rapid, automatic responses to stimuli that bypass conscious thought. The reflex arc: stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron in spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (muscle/gland) → response. Reflexes are fast because they do not involve the brain (at least initially), protecting the body from harm.

notes.heading: The Excretory (Urinary) System
notes.body: The excretory system removes metabolic waste products — primarily urea (from protein breakdown) — and regulates water and salt balance. Kidneys (two bean-shaped organs) filter the blood. Each kidney contains about one million microscopic filtration units called nephrons. In each nephron: (1) Blood enters under high pressure in the glomerulus (a knot of capillaries). (2) Small molecules — water, glucose, salts, urea — are forced out into the Bowman's capsule (ultrafiltration). Large molecules like proteins and blood cells stay in the blood. (3) The filtrate passes through the tubule where selective reabsorption occurs: all glucose, most water, and needed salts are reabsorbed back into the blood. (4) Unwanted substances (excess water, urea, excess salts) remain in the filtrate and form urine. Urine travels from each kidney through a ureter to the bladder (storage) and exits via the urethra. The kidneys also play a vital role in homeostasis — they regulate the water content of blood (osmoregulation) in response to the hormone ADH (anti-diuretic hormone). Common misconception: urine is NOT filtered blood — it is made from filtered blood.

notes.heading: The Skeletal and Muscular Systems
notes.body: The skeletal system has five key functions: support (framework for body), protection (skull protects brain; ribcage protects heart and lungs), movement (muscles pull on bones across joints), mineral storage (calcium and phosphorus), and blood cell production (in bone marrow). Bones are connected at joints, held together by tough, elastic ligaments. Cartilage covers bone ends to reduce friction and acts as a shock absorber. Synovial fluid lubricates the joint. Muscles move bones by contracting (shortening) — they can only pull, never push. This is why muscles work in antagonistic pairs. Example: the biceps and triceps in the upper arm. To bend (flex) the elbow: biceps contracts, triceps relaxes. To straighten (extend) the elbow: triceps contracts, biceps relaxes. Muscles are connected to bones by inelastic tendons. Important: the same muscle cannot simultaneously contract and relax — the action is always coordinated by the nervous system.

notes.heading: How Body Systems Work Together — Homeostasis
notes.body: No body system works in isolation. Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes. Examples of systems collaborating: (1) Exercise: muscles need more energy → increased respiration → more CO₂ produced → detected by brain → increased breathing rate (respiratory) and heart rate (circulatory) to deliver more O₂ and remove CO₂. Body temperature rises → sweating (excretory/skin) and vasodilation (blood vessels near skin widen to lose heat). (2) Eating a meal: digestive system breaks down food → soluble nutrients absorbed into blood (circulatory) → glucose level rises → pancreas releases insulin (hormonal/endocrine) → cells take up glucose → blood glucose returns to normal. (3) Response to danger: sensory neurons detect threat → brain processes fear → adrenal glands release adrenaline (hormonal) → heart rate increases, breathing deepens, pupils dilate, blood diverted to muscles. This demonstrates the nervous-hormonal-circulatory-respiratory systems working together. Key concept: feedback systems — most homeostatic mechanisms use negative feedback (a change triggers a response that reverses the change, e.g., temperature regulation).

flashcards.definition: A biological catalyst — a protein that speeds up a specific chemical reaction without being used up.
flashcards.example: Amylase breaks down starch into maltose in the mouth and small intestine.

flashcards.definition: Millions of tiny finger-like projections lining the small intestine, massively increasing surface area for absorbing digested food into the blood.
flashcards.example: The small intestine has ~200 m² of surface area due to villi and microvilli.

flashcards.definition: Tiny air sacs in the lungs (millions per lung) where gas exchange occurs — O₂ diffuses into blood, CO₂ diffuses out.
flashcards.example: Alveoli walls are one cell thick to minimise the diffusion distance for gases.

flashcards.definition: A blood vessel carrying blood away from the heart at high pressure; has thick muscular and elastic walls with a narrow lumen.
flashcards.example: The aorta is the body's largest artery, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle.

flashcards.definition: Red protein pigment in red blood cells that binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it at respiring tissues.
flashcards.example: Each red blood cell contains about 270 million haemoglobin molecules.

flashcards.definition: A nerve cell specialised for transmitting electrical impulses rapidly over long distances.
flashcards.example: A motor neuron can have an axon up to 1 metre long, carrying signals from the spinal cord to a muscle.

flashcards.definition: The pathway of a reflex action: stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron (CNS) → motor neuron → effector → response. Bypasses conscious brain for speed.
flashcards.example: Touching a hot surface triggers an immediate withdrawal reflex before you even feel the pain.

flashcards.definition: Microscopic filtration unit of the kidney; each kidney contains ~1 million nephrons that filter blood to produce urine.
flashcards.example: Blood enters the glomerulus of each nephron under high pressure for ultrafiltration.

flashcards.definition: Nitrogenous waste product formed in the liver from excess amino acids; removed from blood by the kidneys and excreted in urine.
flashcards.example: High protein diets increase urea production because more amino acids are broken down.

flashcards.definition: A pair of muscles that work together to move a bone — one contracts while the other relaxes. Muscles can only pull, never push.
flashcards.example: Biceps (flexor) and triceps (extensor) are an antagonistic pair controlling the elbow joint.

flashcards.definition: A freely movable joint where bones are separated by a fluid-filled cavity; cartilage reduces friction and ligaments hold bones together.
flashcards.example: The knee, elbow, and shoulder are all synovial joints.

flashcards.definition: The maintenance of a constant internal environment (temperature, water content, blood glucose, pH) despite external changes.
flashcards.example: Shivering warms the body when cold; sweating cools it when hot — both restore normal body temperature (~37°C).

questions.stem: Where does the absorption of digested food mainly occur?
questions.explanation: The small intestine has millions of villi providing a huge surface area for absorbing glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, and glycerol into the blood.

questions.stem: Which enzyme begins digesting starch in the mouth?
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase in saliva starts breaking down starch into maltose while food is being chewed.

questions.stem: What four features make alveoli efficient at gas exchange?
choices: Thick walls, small surface area, dry surface, poor blood supply
Large surface area, thin walls (one cell thick), moist surface, rich blood supply
Medium surface area, thick walls, acidic surface, moderate blood supply
Large surface area, thick muscular walls, dry surface, lymphatic supply
questions.explanation: Alveoli are adapted with huge surface area, extremely thin walls (short diffusion pathway), a moist lining (gases dissolve), and dense capillary networks (maintain concentration gradients).

questions.stem: Where does the right side of the heart pump blood?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs via the pulmonary artery to pick up oxygen.

questions.stem: Which blood vessel carries blood back to the heart and has valves to prevent backflow?
questions.explanation: Veins return blood to the heart at low pressure. Valves inside veins ensure blood flows in one direction only, preventing backflow.

questions.stem: In a reflex arc, why does the response happen before you consciously feel pain?
choices: The brain processes the reflex faster than conscious sensation
The impulse travels only to the spinal cord (relay neuron) and back — bypassing the brain initially
Reflexes are processed in the muscles themselves
Pain signals travel more slowly than motor signals
questions.explanation: The reflex arc goes: receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron in spinal cord → motor neuron → effector. The brain is bypassed for speed; you become aware of pain afterwards.

questions.stem: Which substance is NOT present in the filtrate that enters the Bowman's capsule in a healthy kidney?
questions.explanation: Ultrafiltration in the glomerulus filters out small molecules (water, glucose, salts, urea). Large molecules like proteins and blood cells are too big to pass through and remain in the blood.

questions.stem: Why must the biceps relax when the triceps contracts?
choices: So both muscles can rest alternately
Because muscles work in antagonistic pairs — one must relax for the other to pull the bone in the opposite direction
Because the triceps is stronger and overrides the biceps
To prevent the joint from dislocating
questions.explanation: Muscles can only pull (contract), never push. To extend the arm, the triceps contracts while the biceps relaxes. They are an antagonistic pair.

questions.stem: During exercise, which two body systems work together MOST directly to deliver oxygen to muscles?
questions.explanation: The respiratory system brings oxygen into the lungs, and the circulatory system transports it via the blood to working muscles.

questions.stem: What is the role of bile in digestion?
choices: It emulsifies fats — breaking large fat droplets into smaller ones — increasing surface area for lipase to work
It neutralises stomach acid in the large intestine
questions.explanation: Bile (produced by the liver, stored in the gall bladder) emulsifies fats. It does NOT chemically digest fats — it physically breaks them into smaller droplets so lipase has more surface area to work on.

questions.stem: A person has a high-protein diet. Which excretory product will increase most in their urine?
questions.explanation: Excess amino acids from protein digestion are broken down in the liver, producing urea as a nitrogenous waste product. More protein intake = more urea production and excretion.

questions.stem: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right ventricle wall?
choices: It pumps blood to the lungs which have high resistance
It receives blood from the whole body at high pressure
It must pump blood around the entire body (systemic circulation), requiring greater force
It has to overcome gravity to pump blood to the brain
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body (systemic circulation), needing much greater pressure than the right ventricle, which only pumps to the nearby lungs.

questions.stem: If the air temperature drops to 5°C, which homeostatic response will the body trigger?
choices: Vasodilation — blood vessels widen to lose heat
Shivering — rapid, involuntary muscle contractions generating heat
Decreased metabolic rate to conserve energy
questions.explanation: Shivering generates heat through rapid muscle contractions. The body also triggers vasoconstriction (narrowing blood vessels near the skin) to reduce heat loss.

questions.stem: Which part of a neuron is insulated by the myelin sheath, and what is the benefit?
choices: The dendrites — helps them receive more signals
The cell body — protects the nucleus
The axon — speeds up the transmission of electrical impulses
The axon terminals — helps release more neurotransmitter
questions.explanation: The myelin sheath insulates the axon, allowing electrical impulses to jump between gaps (nodes of Ranvier) — this is called saltatory conduction, and it dramatically increases transmission speed.

questions.stem: A patient has a condition where their kidneys fail to filter blood properly. Which treatment replicates the function of nephrons?
choices: Dialysis — a machine filters the patient's blood outside the body
questions.explanation: Dialysis replicates kidney function by passing the patient's blood through a selectively permeable membrane in a machine. Waste products (urea, excess salts) diffuse out while blood cells and proteins are retained.
